TwitchCam V1

A pan/tilt camera robot that constantly livestreams while Twitch chat controls the experience.

What it is

A camera robot that Twitch chat drives live, inspired by Twitch Plays Pokémon. Viewers type a command like !move_servo 1 90, the camera pans or tilts, and the stream shows the new view. It is meant to always be on.

What I did
  • Split the system between a Raspberry Pi running ROS 2 and the stream, and a Teensy that drives two SG90 servos, linked over UART with micro-ROS.
  • Used a distributed architecture using micro-ROS, ROS2, and multithreading to help parse Twitch chat and convert that to actionable servo action while maintaining a livestream.
  • Wrote the ROS 2 nodes in Python, mainly a chat bot that parses commands and calls a servo service, and a stream node that rotates the camera image, overlays the servo positions with OpenCV and pushes it to Twitch with ffmpeg.
  • Wrote the Teensy firmware (Arduino C++ with micro-ROS): it serves the move request, moves the servo, and replies with where it ended up.
  • Defined custom ROS 2 interfaces for the servo service and position topic, and mapped servo angles to the camera's view so the center is [0, 0] for viewers.
Result
  • Ran for four months straight with no crashes or network drops. Latency mostly comes from the viewer's own connection.
  • Random users from online interacted daily with the robot proving and interactive chat experience.
  • Learn more about designing human robot interaction through a live text-based interface.
  • Next steps became V2: better servos, a proper enclosure, and a portable build.
  • The code is on GitHub: twitch_cam (the ROS 2 nodes) and twitch_cam_msgs (the servo service and message). The channel is twitch.tv/prettygoodengineer.
